baseline: Host Linux 6.8.0 (LTP 20260529) passes all 5 assertions. Per assertion, the correct kernel returns: (1) fsync(pipe write end) = -1/EINVAL; (2) fsync(AF_UNIX SOCK_STREAM fd) = -1/EINVAL; (3) fsync(closed fd) = -1/EBADF; (4) fsync(-1) = -1/EBADF; (5) fsync(fifo fd opened O_WRONLY) = -1/EINVAL. A supplementary host probe written for this run widened the baseline: fifo read end = EINVAL, fifo O_PATH fd = EBADF, regular file = 0, regular O_PATH fd = EBADF, /dev/null = EINVAL, anonymous pipe write end = EINVAL, directory = 0. The rule the baseline encodes is that fsync's success depends on the file's operations vector, not on the inode's type: a file whose operations provide no sync method fails EINVAL, and an fd not open for I/O fails EBADF.
failing_assertion: 2 of 5 assertions fail in Asterinas at 68bdd4a99. qemu.log line 53 (case 1, pipe write end): 'fsync03.c:66: TFAIL: fsync() returned unexpected value 0' where EINVAL was required. qemu.log line 57 (case 5, fifo opened O_WRONLY): 'fsync03.c:66: TFAIL: fsync() returned unexpected value 0' where EINVAL was required. Asterinas' actual wrong value is a successful return of 0 in both cases. Cases 2 (socket, EINVAL), 3 (closed fd, EBADF) and 4 (fd -1, EBADF) pass. Note this contradicts select.json's hypothesis, which predicted the fifo case alone would fail and that the pipe case already passed.
root_cause: sys_fsync (kernel/src/syscall/fsync.rs:9-17) resolves the fd and then uses file.as_inode_handle_or_err()? as its only type gate before calling path.sync_all(). That gate, defined at kernel/src/fs/file/file_handle.rs:273-277, returns EINVAL only when the FileLike is not an InodeHandle at all. It therefore catches sockets, which are a distinct FileLike, but not pipes or fifos, because in Asterinas both of those *are* InodeHandles: kernel/src/fs/pipe/anon_pipe.rs:22-37 (new_file_pair) builds an anonymous pipe as a pair of Arc<InodeHandle> over an AnonPipeInode on PipeFs, and every filesystem opens a named pipe through Pipe::open_named (kernel/src/fs/fs_impls/ramfs/fs.rs:284, kernel/src/fs/fs_impls/ext2/impl_for_vfs/inode.rs:166-169), which yields an InodeHandle whose open_file is a PipeHandle. The downcast consequently succeeds for both, control reaches path.sync_all(), which is inherited from the inode via kernel/src/fs/vfs/path/mod.rs:705, and lands on the blanket default Inode::sync_all at kernel/src/fs/vfs/fs_apis/inode.rs:469-471 that simply returns Ok(()). Neither pseudofs nor ramfs overrides sync_all or sync_data, so nothing on the pipe/fifo path ever rejects the call and sys_fsync returns SyscallReturn::Return(0). The identical mechanism applies to sys_fdatasync (lines 19-27) via sync_data, whose default at inode.rs:473-475 is also Ok(()).
invariant: fsync/fdatasync must fail with EINVAL on a file whose file description provides no synchronization operation - notably pipes, FIFOs and sockets - rather than returning success. A successful fsync is a durability guarantee, so it must never be reported for a file type that has no data to make durable. The decision belongs to the file description's operation set, not to the inode's type, and it must be reached before the request is delegated to the generic inode sync path whose no-op default silently succeeds. Correspondingly, fsync/fdatasync on a descriptor not open for I/O (O_PATH) must fail EBADF.
owning_layer: The per-open file description layer: the PerOpenFileOps trait (kernel/src/fs/file/inode_handle.rs:525-572) together with the InodeHandle method that dispatches to it. PerOpenFileOps is Asterinas' analogue of Linux's struct file_operations - InodeHandle::open_file is documented at inode_handle.rs:31-34 as the counterpart of Linux's file_private - and it already carries exactly this kind of per-file-type veto in check_seekable (inode_handle.rs:527), which PipeHandle overrides at kernel/src/fs/pipe/common.rs:139-142 to reject seeking with ESPIPE. Sync should be gated the same way and dispatched from an InodeHandle method, following the pattern InodeHandle::seek uses at inode_handle.rs:400-418: consult open_file first, then fall back to an inode-type check. Placing the check in PerOpenFileOps rather than in sys_fsync is what makes it correct rather than merely sufficient, because it also covers fdatasync and every future caller, and because it matches the layer at which the baseline shows the distinction actually being made.
linux_reference: Linux enforces this in the VFS, above the filesystem, in fs/sync.c: vfs_fsync_range checks whether the file's operations provide an fsync method and returns -EINVAL when they do not, so the request never reaches the filesystem. The reason pipes and FIFOs hit that path is that fs/pipe.c gives them pipefifo_fops, which deliberately has no .fsync member, and sockets get socket_file_ops in net/socket.c, likewise without .fsync; the fsync(2) man page documents the resulting EINVAL as 'fd is bound to a special file (e.g., a pipe, FIFO, or socket) which does not support synchronization'. The placement is the load-bearing part: the veto lives in the per-file operations table consulted by generic VFS code, which is why a single rule covers fsync and fdatasync and every file type at once. Caveat on method: this container's man pages are stripped and all web reads were blocked by network policy in this environment, so the Linux side could not be re-read from source for this run and is stated from established knowledge; it is corroborated empirically by the host probe above, in which /dev/null returns EINVAL while a directory returns 0 - a split that only a per-operations-vector rule explains, and that an inode-type rule cannot.
other_callers: sync_all/sync_data are reached from outside the filesystem implementations at only three sites: sys_fsync (fsync.rs:15), sys_fdatasync (fsync.rs:25) and sys_msync (kernel/src/syscall/msync.rs:53). sys_fdatasync is affected by exactly the same defect and is not covered by fsync03, so a fix confined to sys_fsync would leave fdatasync(pipe_fd) still wrongly returning 0 - the concrete reason to fix this at the PerOpenFileOps layer rather than in the syscall. sys_msync discards the result with 'let _ =' and only ever operates on mapped file inodes, so it is unaffected either way. sys_syncfs (kernel/src/syscall/sync.rs:19-29) and sys_sync take a different route through FileSystem::sync and are not affected. Two adjacent divergences share the same root and the same owning layer, both outside fsync03's scope: fsync on an O_PATH fd returns 0 in Asterinas where Linux returns EBADF, because sys_fsync goes straight to path.sync_all() and never passes through an InodeHandle method, thereby skipping the rights.is_empty() guard that 12 other InodeHandle operations apply (O_PATH yields (None, Rights::empty()) at inode_handle.rs:58-59); and fsync on /dev/null returns 0 where the host returns EINVAL.
suggested_direction: Add a check_syncable() -> Result<()> method to PerOpenFileOps in kernel/src/fs/file/inode_handle.rs alongside check_seekable, and override it in PipeHandle (kernel/src/fs/pipe/common.rs:139) to return EINVAL - one override that fixes both failing assertions at once, since the anonymous pipe and the named fifo both open as a PipeHandle. Give the trait method a default of Ok(()) so device and procfs per-open files keep their current behaviour; a default of EINVAL would be closer to Linux, where the absence of an .fsync member is the common case, but it would change many device and pseudo-file paths in one step and risks regressing tests outside this one, so it is better proposed separately. Then expose the gate as an InodeHandle method that sys_fsync and sys_fdatasync both call in place of as_inode_handle_or_err()?.path().sync_all(), mirroring InodeHandle::seek at inode_handle.rs:400-418: reject when rights.is_empty() with EBADF, consult open_file.check_syncable() when present, and only then delegate to the inode. Routing both syscalls through that single method is what keeps fdatasync from retaining the bug and incidentally closes the O_PATH EBADF gap. Verify with the default configuration and no workdir override, since fsync03 comes from all.txt (line 450); enable it by uncommenting that line.
